result:
Here's a stream of words, written freely as they come:

The morning light filters through curtains I forgot to close last night, painting amber stripes across the wooden floor where dust motes dance like tiny planets orbiting nothing in particular. I should sweep today, or perhaps tomorrow, or maybe the day after that. The cat watches me from the doorway with the patient judgment of a creature who has seen civilizations rise and fall and knows that none of it matters as much as breakfast.

Coffee. The word itself sounds like a small comfort, a ritual, a reason to stand upright. I press the button and wait for the gurgle and hiss, that familiar percussion that means the day has officially begun, even though it began hours ago when the birds decided to argue outside my window. They always argue. I think it's a territorial thing, or perhaps they're just loud, or perhaps I'm projecting human concerns onto creatures whose motivations are entirely foreign to me. We do that, don't we? We assume everyone thinks like us, feels like us, wants what we want.

The coffee maker beeps. I pour. The steam rises in spirals that mean nothing and everything, depending on how you look at them. Some people see faces in clouds; I see possibilities in coffee steam. Today the steam looks like a question mark, which feels appropriate for a Tuesday, or maybe it's Wednesday. I've lost track. The calendar on the wall says one thing, my body says another, and the two are rarely in agreement.

There's a book on the table I started three weeks ago. The spine is cracked at page forty-seven, a bookmark I suppose. The story concerns a woman who walks into the sea and emerges somewhere else, somewhere impossible, somewhere that might be a metaphor or might be literal. I haven't decided which interpretation I prefer. Part of me wants the magical, the inexplicable, the door in the wall that wasn't there yesterday. Part of me wants the psychological, the careful architecture of grief, the way the mind builds houses out of memory to shelter itself from the weather of the world.

The cat stretches, yawns, and pads across the floor with the self-assurance of a creature who pays no rent. I envy that. The freedom of being small and warm and fed, of not knowing what mortgages are or what climate change means or why the news makes my chest tight every morning. The cat lives entirely in the present tense, which is a tense I find difficult to inhabit. I'm always either regretting the past or rehearsing the future, rarely just here, just this, just coffee and light and the sound of traffic beginning outside.

My phone glows on the counter. Notifications. I won't look yet. The day is too new, too tender, to be filled with other people's urgencies. Let the emails wait. Let the messages pile up like fallen leaves. There will be time enough to rake them later, to sort the meaningful from the noise, to answer the questions that require answering and ignore the ones that don't.

Outside, the neighborhood is waking. Doors opening, cars starting, the distant laughter of someone walking a dog. Ordinary sounds. The kind that compose the symphony of a life being lived by thousands of people simultaneously, each one convinced their own story is the main narrative, their own concerns the central plot. And maybe we're all right. Maybe every life is the main character of its own novel, and we're all just walking through each other's chapters without knowing it.

I think about my grandmother, who died last spring. She used to say that time moves faster when you're older, that the years compress like accordions. I didn't understand then. I think I'm beginning to. The months blur now, the seasons failing to distinguish themselves as sharply as they did when I was young. Summer leaked into fall, fall into winter, winter into this strange in-between space that the calendar insists is spring but my body recognizes as still waiting, still thawing, still uncertain.

The coffee is half gone. The book is still open to page forty-seven. The cat has fallen asleep in a sunbeam, completely surrendered to the present moment. Maybe that's the secret. Maybe wisdom is just learning to be a cat—to eat when hungry, sleep when tired, love without condition, exist without apology. Maybe I've been overthinking this entire time, and the answer was always as simple as fur and whiskers and a purr that sounds like contentment distilled into sound.

I should write something today. Not because I have to, but because the words are there, lined up like passengers waiting for a train, and it would be rude to leave them waiting. They want to go somewhere. They want to become sentences, paragraphs, whole architectures of meaning. Or maybe they just want to exist, to be acknowledged, to know that someone heard them even if no one else ever does.

The light has shifted. The amber stripes have moved across the floor, and the dust motes have rearranged themselves into new constellations. Time is passing. It's always passing. The only question is whether we're passing with it or fighting against it, whether we're swimming in the current or clinging to the bank.

I think I'll have another cup of coffee. I think I'll read a few more pages. I think I'll let the morning be what it is—imperfect, unremarkable, mine. And maybe that's enough. Maybe that's always been enough.
